title: Asking a Team Member to Give Advice to a Peer on the Issue They Need to Work On
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The post proposes a feedback tactic for leaders whose direct feedback has not landed: ask the resistant team member to advise a peer who struggles with the same issue. It rests on the familiar idea that teaching others clarifies one's own thinking. The author describes how to run it, including setting parameters, explaining the peer-teacher role, and holding a three-way session in which the leader lets the advisor speak. The central claim is that people who deflect feedback feel pressure to avoid hypocrisy once they have given advice, so they change their own behavior. The piece closes by noting that we advise others better than ourselves, a quirk good leaders occasionally use to produce a breakthrough.
points: Learning by teaching is turned into a feedback strategy for team members who resist direct coaching.
The team member need not recognize that they share the peer's problem for the technique to work.
The leader's discipline matters: set clear parameters and let the advisor give the advice without being run over.
The mechanism is cognitive dissonance, since people feel compelled to follow advice they have just given.
quotes: It is well-known that when people teach others, they achieve a personal clarity that informs their own thinking on the subject. Sharing what they know requires team members to distill their knowledge and explain it in a way that others can easily follow.

In the workplace, the idea of learning by teaching can be a powerful tool for leaders, especially when they have offered feedback to a team member who isn’t getting it or is resistant to change. One strategy available to leaders is to ask team members to give advice and feedback to peers who struggle with the same issues they do.

The key is to discuss the parameters for giving the advice, making sure they understand the role they play as peer and teacher. Leaders who use this strategy often bring both parties together and have a three-way advice session. In the case of a leader engaging in this conversation with the peers, it is essential they allow the team members to offer the advice and not to run over them.

Asking those who deflect feedback to give advice to others helps them to think through the avenues for changing their own actions. Better yet, they become conflicted when they don’t follow the advice they give to others. To avoid being a hypocrite, they are compelled to change their behavior so as to match the recommendations to others.

We normally advise others better than we advise ourselves. Good leaders use this idea to their advantage on occasion. Asking a team member to share their advice with a peer on an issue they need to work on can create a breakthrough moment.
